samples.question: The picture is a plain page divided, from top to bottom, into four horizontal bands of exactly equal height; no line is drawn between them. Counting downwards the bands are the first, second, third and fourth. Each band holds one station. A station is made of two separate square-ish clusters of twelve short straight strokes each: the two clusters of a station are drawn in the same ink colour, they stand side by side in that band with a wide band of empty background between them, and no mark joins them. Every stroke inside one cluster has the same tilt, so a cluster shows a single stroke direction twelve times over. A tilt has no arrowhead: a stroke and the same stroke turned by a half turn point the same way. Exactly one station has both of its clusters tilted the same way, so that the strokes of its left cluster are parallel to the strokes of its right cluster. In every other station the two clusters are tilted clearly differently. Both clusters of a station must be read: one cluster alone never decides anything. Clusters that belong to different bands are never a match, and the page always contains a cluster in some other band whose tilt copies the winning tilt exactly, so a tilt that appears again elsewhere on the page does not name a band. The ink colours, which is only there to show which two clusters belong to the same station, how far the stations sit from the left edge, the small up and down shifts of the stations, and the tiny isolated specks dotted about the background all carry no information. Which band holds the station whose two clusters of strokes are parallel to each other? Answer with one of: first, second, third, fourth.
